title: Hausdorff distance between semialgebraic sets
formal:
Is the following Hausdorff-distance decision language complete for \(\forall\exists\mathbb R\) under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions?

An input consists of a dimension \(n\ge1\), two quantifier-free formulas \(\varphi,\psi\) in \(n\) real variables using integer polynomial equations, strict inequalities and Boolean connectives, and a rational threshold \(t\). The formulas define
\[
A=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\varphi(x)\},\qquad B=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\psi(x)\}.
\]
The formulas are explicitly written finite expression trees; their encodings, including every coefficient, are part of the input. Dimension, degrees and coefficient lengths are variable. No boundedness, closedness, convexity, nonemptiness or fixed-dimensional promise is imposed.

For arbitrary sets in this space define the directed distance and symmetric Hausdorff distance by
\[
\delta(A,B)=\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{b\in B}\|a-b\|_2,
\qquad h(A,B)=\max\{\delta(A,B),\delta(B,A)\},
\qquad\|v\|_2=\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{n}v_i^2\Bigr)^{1/2}.
\]
The extrema are in the extended nonnegative reals, with empty supremum zero and empty infimum infinity. Thus two empty sets have distance zero, exactly one empty set gives infinite distance, and unbounded sets may have either finite or infinite distance. The language \(H\) contains exactly the valid encoded inputs with \(t\ge0\) and \(h(A,B)\le t\); malformed encodings and negative thresholds are rejected.

Let \(U\) be the language of true sentences \(\forall x\in\mathbb R^p\ \exists y\in\mathbb R^q:\theta(x,y)\), with a quantifier-free matrix of the same syntax and explicit finite encoding. Define \(\forall\exists\mathbb R\) as the class of languages polynomial-time many-one reducible to \(U\). The question is precisely whether
\[
H\le_m^{\mathrm P}U\quad\text{and}\quad U\le_m^{\mathrm P}H.
\]
All reductions are single uniform deterministic machines, with worst-case polynomial time in the complete binary input length and exact preservation of membership.

This recovers the exact decision and completeness question in the work cited as reference 13 by the 2020 source: Dobbins, Kleist, Miltzow and Rzążewski explicitly specify a rational threshold and ask for this completeness classification. The preserved 2020 quotation paraphrases that issue as polynomial-time computability. Completeness is a resolved classification and implies a polynomial-time decision algorithm exists exactly when \(\mathrm P=\forall\exists\mathbb R\); it does not prove an unconditional separation from \(\mathrm P\).

source_formulation.text: However, the question whether a polynomial time algorithm exists to compute the Hausdorff distance between general semialgebraic sets remains open [13].

why: Hausdorff distance is a standard way to compare shapes, and implicit polynomial descriptions cover far more than finite point sets. Its classification provides a geometric complete problem for the second universal-existential level of real complexity, identifying how variable dimension and quantified nearest-point conditions affect exact computation.
status_note: Resolved as the explicit classification question in the original cited work. Jungeblut–Kleist–Miltzow’s2023 journal theorem proves strict-universal-existential completeness, and Schaefer–Štefankovič’s unbounded-signature equality yields full universal-existential completeness. Their corrected author version of 3 March 2025 retains this result despite restricting separate bounded-closed-domain claims. The review read the actual definitions, matching reduction and the relevant corrected proof chain, with the encoding details and limits recorded; no Lean proof or independent reconstruction of the external real-algebraic estimates is claimed. The preserved2020 polynomial-time paraphrase is not an unconditional theorem that no polynomial algorithm exists: the decision problem lies in P exactly if P equals the stated real complexity class. Review cutoff 16 September 2026.

progress.text: The full author version of Dobbins and coauthors explicitly defines the rational-threshold Hausdorff decision problem and asks whether it is \(\forall\exists\mathbb R\)-complete.
The ISAAC paper records polynomial-time computation for general semialgebraic sets as an unresolved background issue and cites the earlier classification question.

The published journal version of Jungeblut, Kleist and Miltzow proves that the threshold decision problem is complete for the strict-inequality variant \(\forall\exists_{<}\mathbb R\). Its reduction already produces nonempty sets, and its consequences include NP-hardness and conditional multiplicative inapproximability.
Schaefer and Štefankovič publish the equality \(\forall\exists_{<}\mathbb R=\forall\exists\mathbb R\), yielding the full classification asked for in the original source.

The corrected sixth author version retains the unbounded-signature equality and expressly retains Hausdorff completeness. It retracts or restricts separate higher-level bounded-closed-signature claims, so those stronger statements are not used here.

sentences: Hausdorff distance measures the largest nearest-point discrepancy between two sets in both directions.
The source cited by the 2020 paper explicitly asks for the complexity classification of deciding whether two semialgebraic sets have distance at most a rational threshold.
The model uses exact polynomial formulas, variable dimension and finite bit encodings, including nonclosed and unbounded sets.
Later published work and its corrected author version establish completeness for the universal-existential theory of the reals.
The historical classification is resolved, while its consequence for polynomial-time solvability remains conditional on the corresponding complexity-class equality.

definitions:
The underlying field is the ordinary real field, the ambient metric is the Euclidean metric in the supplied coordinates, and the comparison includes equality. Infima and suprema need not be attained. Sets given by Boolean combinations of polynomial equations and inequalities are called semialgebraic. The input specifies their formulas, rather than an oracle, a list of sampled points, a quantified projection description, a shared arithmetic circuit, or arbitrary real constants. There is no transformation or alignment of the two sets before measuring their distance.

Here is a concrete finite encoding. All characters mentioned below are their ordinary eight-bit ASCII representations, concatenated without whitespace. Unsigned binary integers have no leading zeros, with zero represented by the one-character string 0. A signed integer is a plus or minus sign followed by an unsigned magnitude; zero has the unique representation +0. An integer term is c followed by parentheses around such a signed integer. A variable term is x followed by parentheses around the positive binary index of the variable. If r and s are terms, a(r,s), s(r,s), and m(r,s) are respectively their sum, difference and product. These are recursive syntax trees, with every occurrence written out; no sharing, exponent symbol, macro, division operation or additional arithmetic operation is permitted in a term. In particular, an exponent used in mathematical notation abbreviates repeated explicit multiplication. Binary integer literals are permitted because they can equivalently be expressed with a polynomial number of constant-zero, constant-one and arithmetic symbols.

If r and s are terms, l(r,s) is the atom r strictly less than s, and e(r,s) is the atom r equal to s. If F and G are formulas, n(F), j(F,G), and o(F,G) respectively mean negation, conjunction and disjunction. These rules generate all and only the allowed quantifier-free formulas. Weak inequalities and all other comparison symbols are expressible using these rules. A rational threshold consists of a signed binary numerator, a slash, and a positive unsigned binary denominator in lowest terms. In particular its denominator is one when the numerator is zero.

A unary count is the character 1 repeated exactly that many times. A Hausdorff input is the positive unary dimension, a semicolon, its first formula, a semicolon, its second formula, a semicolon, and the rational threshold. Both formulas may use only variable indices from one through that dimension. A U input consists of the unary count p, a semicolon, the unary count q, a semicolon, and its matrix formula. Empty unary counts represent zero, so either quantifier block may be empty. Variable indices one through p are universally quantified and the next q indices are existentially quantified; no other variable indices are allowed. The interpretation of a zero-length real block is the unique empty tuple. A bitstring that is not a sequence of complete eight-bit characters or does not parse according to the relevant complete-input grammar is outside the respective language. Input length is the number of bits in the whole representation. The explicit unary dimensions and syntax choices are editorial encoding conventions within the source's bit model, not additional algebraic promises. Coordinates absent from both Hausdorff formulas can be removed simultaneously, keeping one dummy coordinate if none remain; variables absent from a U matrix can likewise be omitted without affecting its truth.

For an empty source set the directed distance is zero; for a nonempty source and empty target it is infinity. This explicitly extends the usual definition, which the later source initially states for nonempty sets. It makes H a total language and agrees with the two directed approximation conditions used in the cited quantifier formulation. The proved hardness already uses nonempty sets, so this convention does not create the hardness result. The convention also avoids any hidden promise whose verification might itself require solving a real-feasibility problem. A finite nonnegative rational is always smaller than infinity. Negative thresholds are rejected even for two empty sets.

A deterministic machine is a finite description of an ordinary multitape Turing machine, with a fixed finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a read-only binary input tape, finitely many work tapes and a binary output tape. Each transition reads and writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. Runtime counts every transition, including arithmetic, parsing and output. A reduction has positive integer constants C and k, independent of the input string, and halts on every string s in at most \(C(|s|+1)^k\) steps. It prints one complete binary output string r and must satisfy \(s\in L\Longleftrightarrow r\in K\) to reduce L to K. It has no advice, randomness, real-number registers, nondeterminism or oracle. Output length is included in the running-time bound. Malformed strings have the language membership specified above, so reduction correctness is a statement about all binary strings, not just syntactically valid inputs.

The notation \(L\le_m^{\mathrm P}K\) means that such a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction exists. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of binary languages decidable by one uniform deterministic machine within such a bound. Completeness for \(\forall\exists\mathbb R\) means membership in that class together with hardness for every language in it. Because U defines the class, this is equivalent to the two displayed reductions. This is a discrete bit-complexity classification, not a real-arithmetic machine classification. No assumption that \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), or that either real complexity class is distinct from another, forms part of the completeness assertion.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the two-reduction assertion, or a complete Lean proof of its logical negation, for the languages and encodings defined above.

For languages L and K, a finite machine M, positive integers C and k, and a binary string s, let \(G_{L,K}(M,C,k,s)\) mean that the run halts within \(C(|s|+1)^k\) transitions with a binary output r and that \(s\in L\Longleftrightarrow r\in K\). The positive assertion is
\[
\exists M,N\ \exists C,D,k,\ell\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \forall s\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad
G_{H,U}(M,C,k,s)\ \wedge\ G_{U,H}(N,D,\ell,s).
\]
Its exact negation is
\[
\forall M,N\ \forall C,D,k,\ell\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\ \exists s\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad
\neg G_{H,U}(M,C,k,s)\ \vee\ \neg G_{U,H}(N,D,\ell,s).
\]
The machines and constants are chosen before all input strings. A positive proof must establish both uniform polynomial-time transformations and both directions of each membership equivalence on the entire stated domain. A negative proof must exclude the existence of a pair of valid reductions; failure of a particular published construction is insufficient. Completeness for a smaller class without proving its equality with the stated class, a randomized or oracle reduction, or a theorem assuming a complexity-class separation does not establish the requested classification. An approximate real output or a numerical tolerance is not an answer to this exact decision-class question. The historical classification is already resolved in the cited literature; the Lean requirement specifies what a formally certified answer to the recorded statement would mean and does not assert an existing Lean development.

Substantive proof caution: v6 Proposition 2.6 equation(6), PDF 15, has a problematic small-y0 versus increasing-chain expression; do not use that stronger single-degree-six normal form as a verified dependency. The needed Theorem 1.2 only requires a strict Boolean formula. Its exponentially large power can be encoded in polynomial size by a strict decreasing squaring chain: universally quantify unrestricted real z, existentially choose u0>0 with (1+z^2)*u0<1, 0<ui<u(i-1)^2, |g(x)|<um and |u0*xj|<1 with 2^m>=C. A true root admits a sufficiently small u0 and positive chain for every z; conversely um<u0^(2^m)<=u0^C and arbitrarily large z yield Theorem 2.4’s condition for every positive tolerance. All domains remain unrestricted and every atom is strict, with no non-strict guard hidden in forall z>0. This supplies the elementary encoding detail without relying on the questionable optional equation. The external effective Lojasiewicz theorem underlying Theorem 2.4 was not independently reconstructed or Lean-formalized. Detailed audit saved /tmp/atlas-audit-5875.md.

Additional source cautions, unnecessary for the general-threshold resolution: v6PDF 3 accidentally calls symmetric Hausdorff the minimum, whereas its next displayed formula uses maximum and JKM’s definition is maximum. Use maximum. v6PDF 42’s auxiliary zero-distance proof suppresses a cube-to-ball norm normalization; use the primary JKM nonempty-set reduction plus Theorem 1.2 for the main disposition instead. The zero-threshold theorem is literature context, not an extra theorem required by this card. Closed sets at threshold zero reduce to equality and have a different classification; do not silently impose closedness at that endpoint.

Total-language audit: use extended nonnegative extrema with sup(empty)=0,inf(empty)=infinity. The directed Hausdorff approximation condition is universally quantified over source points with a separate implication for each direction, so two empty sets satisfy it and exactly one empty set fails it. Never combine both source memberships into one antecedent, which would be vacuous for exactly one empty set. Negative rational thresholds are NO. General threshold membership remains a polynomial-size universal-existential formula. This is an editorial totalization of the source’s initial nonempty-set definition, and the main hardness maps every valid source instance to nonempty sets.
